claims.claim: Courts resolve disputes by determining the facts of a case and applying the law to those facts; the U.S. district courts' official description states that district courts 'conduct trials and hearings, resolving disputes by determining the facts and applying the law to those facts.'

The Supreme Court is the highest tribunal in the nation for all cases and controversies arising under the Constitution or the laws of the United States, and functions as final arbiter, guardian, and interpreter of the Constitution.
Article III, Section 1 vests the judicial power of the United States in one supreme Court and in such inferior courts as Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.

The federal judiciary is organized in three tiers: 94 district (trial) courts with at least one in each state, 13 courts of appeals (12 regional circuits plus the Federal Circuit), and the Supreme Court at the top.

Trial courts are where cases start: witnesses testify, evidence and arguments are presented; appellate courts review lower-court decisions and do not retry cases, hear new evidence, hear witnesses, or use juries.
A civil case begins with pleadings: the plaintiff files a complaint stating the claim and the relief sought, and the defendant responds with an answer asserting defenses.

A party who loses at trial may appeal; the appellate court reviews the lower court's decision and may change it, but the losing party has no right to have the Supreme Court hear the appeal — the Court's review is discretionary, granted through a writ of certiorari when at least four of the nine justices vote to accept the case (the Rule of Four).

Article III, Section 1 protects judicial independence: judges 'shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour' (effectively lifetime tenure) and 'shall, at stated Times, receive for their Services, a Compensation, which shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office.'

The Constitution limits the courts to deciding actual 'Cases' and 'Controversies': the Court does not give advisory opinions, its function is limited to deciding specific cases, and Chief Justice John Jay declined early on to advise President Washington on a proposed foreign policy decision.

Standing is the requirement that a party bringing a lawsuit demonstrate a sufficient connection to, and harm from, the law or action being challenged; legal actions cannot be brought simply because someone is displeased with a law or action.

The Court's term begins by law on the first Monday in October; each term approximately 5,000-7,000 new cases are filed, and the Court grants plenary review in only about 80 of them, disposing of roughly 100 or more without plenary review.

The Court's power to invalidate legislation or executive actions that conflict with the Constitution — judicial review — was confirmed in 1803 in Marbury v. Madison, when Chief Justice John Marshall asserted that the Court's responsibility to overturn unconstitutional legislation followed from its sworn duty to uphold the Constitution; the doctrine itself is covered in the sibling judicial-review topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many cases the Supreme Court accepts each term: the Court's own 'Supreme Court at Work' page reports about 80 granted plenary review out of roughly 5,000-7,000 filed, while the uscourts.gov 'Supreme Court Procedures' page reports 100-150 accepted of more than 7,000 asked.
positions: supremecourt.gov: approximately 5,000-7,000 new cases filed each term, about 80 granted plenary review
uscourts.gov: more than 7,000 petitions asked, 100-150 accepted
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the Court's own figures (5,000-7,000 filed; about 80 granted plenary review) because the primary institution reporting its own caseload is the authoritative source for that number; the discrepancy is noted here and no intermediate figure is taught.
